text.what: A triangular two-to-five-pound piece of bottom sirloin, rolled in salt, pepper and garlic, grilled over red oak coals to medium-rare and sliced across the grain. In its home valley it arrives with pinquito beans, salsa, green salad and buttered French bread grilled on the same fire.
text.story: The barbecue is older than the cut. Californio ranchers fed their vaqueros each spring from oak-coal pits, and the Santa Maria Club ran a stag barbecue for up to 700 people a month from 1931. Top sirloin was the meat. In the late 1950s a market manager in Santa Maria put a triangular piece that usually went to the grinder on a rotisserie instead, and by the 1960s the town had a cut of its own.
text.how: Grill directly over red oak, fat side up, turning once; pull at 130–135 °F and let it rest before slicing. The grain changes direction inside the muscle, so the knife has to change with it. Central California butchers leave the fat cap on; butchers elsewhere trim it.
text.today: Sold country-wide now, and still the default thing to cook at a Santa Maria Valley fundraiser, rodeo or school benefit.

kin.as: The long version: the ranch, the oak, the competing claims, and the wine question.
The wood, which is not a red oak.
The valley that also grows pinot noir on the same hills.
The market manager the town credits.
Which defines the phrase on the menu.
